title: Meet the winner of Nikon's Small World in Motion video contest
gist: Tsinghua University optical engineer Ning Xu won Nikon's 2026 Small World in Motion competition with a diffractive super-resolution microscopy video of abnormal cilia beating in a child with a rare genetic respiratory disorder, using a low-light imaging technique that avoids damaging living samples.

insights.claim: Winner Ning Xu captured abnormal beating of airway cilia in a child with Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia using diffractive super-resolution microscopy, a technique employing multiple lightwaves and a digital micromirror to precisely shape light while minimizing exposure to the living sample.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Diffractive super-resolution microscopy's low-light, high-resolution capability on living samples is a specific imaging technique advancement relevant to researchers and instrument makers targeting live-cell diagnostics for rare genetic disorders.

insights.claim: Studying Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia requires observing roughly 10 seconds of cilia motion rather than still imagery, which rules out many advanced microscopy techniques that rely on intense light or fluorescent dyes because the sample must remain alive and undamaged during imaging.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The specific technical constraint (motion capture on living, undamaged samples) defines why this imaging niche remains underserved by conventional fluorescent/high-intensity microscopy methods, a gap this winning technique addresses.

insights.claim: Ning Xu's entry beat out 346 other video submissions from 40 different countries to win the 2026 Small World in Motion competition, a video-focused spinoff of Nikon's Small World Photomicrography Competition that has run since 1974.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Scale figures (346 entries, 40 countries) establish the competition's global reach as a recurring benchmark event in scientific microscopy imaging, useful context for tracking year-over-year growth in the field.

insights.claim: Runners-up included researchers from Vietnam, Germany, the US (Howard Hughes Medical Institute), and Scotland, covering subjects from roundworm motion to synchronized cell division and mitochondria/chloroplast dynamics in plant cells.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A geographically and topically diverse runner-up field signals broad international participation in advanced live-cell microscopy research across academic and independent labs.
